utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-03-69-T, The Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. As everyone will see, Judge Picard is not present at this moment. She is unable to continue sitting for urgent personal reasons. And Judge Gwaunza and myself are satisfied that it's in the interests of justice to continue hearing this case. I add to this, that the absence of Judge Picard is likely to be of a short duration. So, therefore, we have -- we hereby order that the hearing of the case continue in the absence of Judge Picard. Apart from that, I established that Mr. Stanisic is not present in court. We are waiting for a filled-in waiver form, but since we discussed his absence already yesterday, we could continue even when that form has not yet arrived. Mr. Jordash, I take it that the waiver of his right to be present, which was expressed yesterday, is unchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then is the witness available to be brought into the courtroom? Mr. Groome, you'll have a -- later today an opportunity to address the matter you wished to address.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Harbour, yesterday you said a session or perhaps even less than a session. That's still your estimate?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Selak. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, as I did yesterday, I again remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you've given at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Harbour, are you ready to continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, yesterday it became clear that you're very familiar with the proceedings before this Tribunal and you reviewed many of the documents that have been used in various proceedings. I'd ask that in response to my questions today, if you could please limit your answers to what you know from your own personal experience and observations at the time that we're discussing rather than referring to information that you learned subsequently from various documents. And if you do find it absolutely necessary to refer to those documents to fully respond to a question, could you please clearly indicate that your answer relates to information gleaned from documents rather than your personal knowledge at the time?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: You've testified about your involvement as logistics commander and supplying, weapons, ammunition and other equipment to JNA and TO units in Croatia. Was any paperwork required in order to move across borders from one republic to another in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No paperwork was needed, except for official military documents accompanying consignments of military equipment, indicating to which unit and how much.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Were there any passes that needed to be issued to the convoys before they could cross the borders, or anything to that effect?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about any passes because where military equipment was delivered, where military units were located, there were authorities of Yugoslavia in power; later Republika Srpska. So I don't know of any passes. There was just military documentation indicating what is carried, to whom, and how much. I never had any special laissez-passer.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: In your comments chart, which is now in evidence as D730, you commented on three documents from April 1992 that reflected the SSNO ordering the ammunition -- the issuing of ammunition to the Serbian Krajina MUP via the 2nd Military District. You commented that: "It was quite normal for police to request from the army this kind of supplies." And my question for you is: Do you know anything about the Serbian MUP's involvement in issuing ammunition to the Serbian Krajina MUP?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no specific information about that. There was information about deliveries of police equipment, not military equipment, but that didn't go through the logistics base in Banja Luka, so I have no specific information what was delivered and at what time because that would be in the documentation of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia. It would be been the Serbian MUP and the Republika Srpska MUP. I didn't have any documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: You have provided evidence in your Milosevic testimony at transcript page 22328 and 22344 through -46, that the JNA was involved in arming the Serb TO in Western Slavonia and that the JNA and TO were involved in various combat operations in that area of Croatia in Pakrac, in Lipik, in 1991. Do you know what the Serbian DB's role in Western Slavonia was during that time?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbian state security made efforts to organise authorities and the system of government in that area in Republika Srpska, so it was quite logical for the police to do their job. The army did not interfere with that, and it operated in the only way possible at the time. It was between municipalities and the MUPs of municipalities and their police forces where the army had to get involved with deliveries of equipment, materiel, and perhaps ammunition. That was done quite legally, and it went on quite normally.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: When I refer to the Serbian DB, I refer to the State Security Service of the Republic of Serbia. Is that also how you interpreted my question and how we should interpret your response?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have any contacts or any precise information about the contacts of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia with the MUP of Republika Srpska. I did not have access to that sort of information. All that I know is from my contacts with the security organs in Banja Luka, so I wouldn't be able to tell you anything about that. There were contacts, but what was the -- the issue, they -- they dealt with between them, and in what way, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Harbour, the first question you put to the witness, you said: "You've testified about your involvement as logistics commander in supplying weapons, ammunition, and other equipment to JNA and TO units in Croatia." Now if my recollection is well, yesterday the main issue and, therefore, I wanted to make sure there was no confusion, the main transport of weapons was those pulled out from Slovenia and Croatia to Bosnia; and, then, later, the transport through the corridor from Serbia to, well, let's say the Banja Luka area. I just want to make sure that the witness understood exactly what you meant by the supply of weapons, ammunition, and other equipment to JNA and TO units in Croatia, because most of what was said yesterday, as far as I remember, was about the movement of supplies, as I just explained. Could you please verify with the witness, and perhaps give us the exact sources and perhaps make sure that -- perhaps by quoting the exact lines what you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: The source that I'm referring to, Mr. Selak, is not your testimony from yesterday which largely focussed on what the Chamber has just mentioned. But, rather, I'd like to focus you on the JNA operations in Western Slavonia --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: -- particularly in the latter portion of 1991. Do you know what the Serbian DB's role, the State Security Service of the Republic of Serbia, what their role was in that part of Croatia, in Western Slavonia, at that time?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't answer the first question about that Territorial Defence unit in Slavonia and logistics base. The base did deliver ammunition and weapons to units of Territorial Defence in Slavonia. I have no knowledge about what the state security of Serbia did in the territory of Slavonia. They were involved around Vukovar. But Pakrac and Lipik, I was present there when the fighting went on. There was a rocket brigade from Banja Luka, one artillery battalion that targeted Pakrac and Lipik; I know that. But about the State Security of Serbia, its role and its activities in Slavonia, I really don't know, and I couldn't have stated that in the Milosevic case because I certainly did not have that kind of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And when you answered the question about the paperwork that was needed, were you referring to the paperwork needed in order to get this equipment into Slavonia; or did you -- were talking about other -- other supplies of weapons? You said no paperwork, just official military documents, where it should be sent, et cetera. Were you then specifically talking about shipments to Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, that documentation was purely military documentation. Police organs in that territory and those were military vehicles with military markings and military escort, did not interfere with that, nor dared to interfere because the army was, of course, stronger. But the civilian authorities functioned normally, so the military transport went without any problem to Slavonia and even the Serbian Krajina; Knin, which, for instance was not in Slavonia. Those were the deliveries. The only problem was their requests were enormous, and I didn't allow for it, because then the weapons would be distributed house to house, and I tried -- I was trying to stop that, to prevent that. There were no other passes, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Could we please now turn to Exhibit P2452. And I note that this document does not need to be under seal, as we indicated in our 2nd of February, 2012, submission.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: This is signed by Jovica Stanisic to the minister of defence of Serbia personally on the 9th of December, 1991. Mr. Selak, was the minister of defence of Serbia Tomislav Simovic at the time?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I can't remember which date it was exactly, so I -- I don't know. I don't know when that was.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: In this document, Stanisic reports information that he received from the TO and police of Western Slavonia. He informs the minister of defence that: "The JNA reservists are leaving positions en masse and withdrawing towards Bijela Stijena and Okucani. The brigade command does not control the situation." And then Stanisic concludes by stating: "Unless adequate support is provided, there's a danger that the soldiers and inhabitants will leave the territory of Western Slavonia." Mr. Selak, do you know if, after this date, the minister of defence made arrangements to supply weapons or any other support to the TO in Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Ministry of the Interior had no need to send weapons to Western Slavonia because there was so many weapons there. People who abandoned their positions, such as deserters, could not carry their weapons with them. Those weapons would remain behind. And after this date, complete units withdrew from Slavonia. The JNA was pulling out from Pakrac and Lipik. Your Honours, allow me to expand on this case because I attended the meeting in General Uzelac's office when he got a call from Belgrade and orders to stop combat in Western Slavonia immediately. That's the area from Pakrac and Lipik towards the Hungarian border. When the phone call ended Uzelac said, I meant to go as far as the Hungarian border but now I can't. And then the pull-out followed. I don't know the exact date, but the JNA pulled out, and the Croatian forces were stronger and stronger all the time. So the army just left the corridor open towards Brcko and towards Serbia, and that corridor was opened all through the war. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I'm going to ask Mr. Laugel to play an excerpt of an intercepted conversation between Mr. Jovica Stanisic and Radovan Karadzic on the 14th of December, 1991. This is in evidence as P673. And Your Honour, I note that the English translation is dated the 4th of December, 1991, whereas the original has the date of 14 December, so I will submit this translation for correction. The intercept is under seal because the transcript bears the signature of an operative but there is no reason that the intercept itself cannot be played publicly. This intercept is about three and a half minutes long. And I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Harbour, I didn't understand the previous answer to be a real answer to your question. I don't know whether you consider that your question has been answered, the previous one, or that you're not interested to hear the answer. The question was whether the witness knows whether any arrangements were made. He explained that there was no need to send weapons, et cetera, but that is all opinion rather than ...

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Let me just clarify with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, I took your previous response to mean that, no, you did not know that any arrangements were made for supply of weapons or other support by the minister of defence to the Western Slavonia region? Was that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's -- at least an answer. He doesn't know, neither in the positive nor in the negative sense. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I would like to ask Mr. Laugel now to play this intercept from the 14th of December, 1991, which is P673. And since we were not able to sync the subtitles to the intercept, I have hard copies of the translation if the Chamber or either of the parties are interested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, have you provided the transcripts to the booth.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's most important. Then I think we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Here's what it is about, the news is pretty controversial from other there in Slavonia. "From Banja Luka. "From Banja Luka. 5.000 new people have arrived in Banja Luka, 10.000 arrive tomorrow. I don't know why they are leaving, those, those villages. Colonel Talic tells me that all of Seselj's men put up a fantastic fight. Before they started sowing defeatism and saying that Serbia had betrayed them, why should they wait there, it would be lost anyway so they killed the fucking lot. "No doctor, don't, don't. "Fall for ... no, no, first they blame 50 of Seselj's men, or 100 Seselj's Men. "Yes, yes. "We have to be an organised state to save this fucking people. "Yes, yes. I am, sort of .... "For them, everyone is to blame, fuck them. "Yes. "When things are bad, the only ones to blame are Seselj's Men and ... "Yes. He says that, he says that they are listening to them and they are in disarray, that they are short of 1.000 to 2.000 men to completely crush them, they, he says, we are listening to them, they, we know for a fact that they are in disarray. They are no good, he say. And we need ... and I told them so, is to set up a brigade there, which is waiting in Bosanski Petrovac, people at home are ready to go, 700, I can raise them in two hours. "Doctor ... "I can raise them. "Doctor, my information over the last three days says that the army is not in control of the situation. "In Western Slavonia. "Yes, yes, they are not in control of the situation. "Yes. Well, who is fighting over there? What is going on? "The army ... but the Territorial Defence is in disarray. "Yes. "They are on the offensive and I think that my information is correct. "Yes, yes. "And that this has been going on for four to five days already. "And what can be done about it? "Well, I told you when you were in Belgrade that I had raised as many as I could and warned their prime minister and the others of the situation. "Yes. "There has to be a military reaction. There has to be a military reaction. "But Talic ... Colonel Talic tells me, we only need a few men to crush them completely because they're falling apart. He says that the Territorial Defence is poor, it's in disarray, but ... he says that the army has not withdrawn a single metre anywhere, by a single metre anywhere, on the territory that the army controls. "What they did hold ... where they had got to, Pakrac, the day before yesterday. "Yes. "You understand. "Yes, yes. "This means that they didn't have a front to speak of up there. "They got as far as Pakrac. Up there our villages, man, they are villages there, from Podravska Slatina, from Bocina Gora. Everybody has moved out from Mount Bilogora, there is no one to protect them from that side, man, there were territorials there, there's no army there, that's the problem. "You see. "Yes, yes. "This means, that ... they didn't have a front up there. "Fucking hell. What are we do to? I really don't know what to do here. "What is to be done ... "Mr. Uzelac is out in the field there. I don't know whereabouts. I can't get a hold of him. "No matter, here, I will ring Belgrade now. I'll call as many people as I can, I mean, but ... it will be a real exodus, man. "Well, yes, I mean, but no Slavonia must be held ... "Are you informed about what they're doing to you here in Banja Luka? "To be honest, I didn't want to go, or to know. If Babic shits there, I'll tell him to go fuck himself. They will probably try to do something stupid, and this Andjelko. "I barely convinced Hadzic not to go there. "Who? "Goran Hadzic. "Who? "Goran, Goran. "Who? "Hadzic. "Ah, right."

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, this -- what you've just heard is an intercept of a conversation between Jovica Stanisic and Radovan Karadzic. And, as I said, this is on the 14th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: In it conversation, Stanisic has told Karadzic about the issue in Western Slavonia. Would you agree that Stanisic appears to be well-informed about the JNA and TO operations in Western Slavonia from this discussion?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Stanisic indicates that prior to this discussion he had warned "their prime minister and the others of the situation." Does this demonstrate his connections with the Serb leadership in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to that question. It's -- it's -- it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're asking the witness to draw conclusions from a text he has heard and seen. Now, you can ask the witness whether he has any personal knowledge about the relationship between -- but to say whether this demonstrates or not is finally a conclusion to be drawn by the Bench. Unless the witness has some specific knowledge about it, then you can ask him for that. But don't ask him to interpret the conversation as such. Your first question was the same, I let it go, but then Mr. Jordash rightly objected to the second question. And I take it that you did that after you had considered to do the same for the first question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Harbour. So if the witness knows anything about how and -- Mr. Stanisic, what kind of knowledge he had about the situation in the -- in Western Slavonia or how he had obtained that knowledge, fine. But to ask whether this document shows it, that's really not for a witness to do. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, as we've discussed, Stanisic has indicated - in this discussion at least - that he had warned the prime minister, their prime minister. Do you have any personal knowledge about any relationship Mr. Stanisic may have had about -- with Serb leadership in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the mass media in Banja Luka reported on the developments in Croatia, specifically in the Serbian Krajina, in Croatia, and the Bosnian Krajina. We knew on this basis and I knew from military sources that these military and political communications were always ongoing with Banja Luka, Belgrade, and the Krajina. And I stand by what I say, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's not about your knowledge. It is about whether you know anything about how Mr. Stanisic gained knowledge of what happened over there, and whether you have any personal knowledge of Mr. Stanisic's communication with the Belgrade leaders. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any knowledge about that. Not personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Harbour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Just to clarify, and you also don't have personal knowledge of Mr. Stanisic's communications with leadership in Croatia, in the Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: In this discussion, Karadzic refers to Talic and Uzelac as being involved in this operation. You knew that the 5th Corps of the JNA was involved in this action. At this point in 1991, what was Dr. Karadzic's authority or relationship over the 5th Corps?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point in time, Karadzic had no powers whatsoever over the 5th Corps, because it was the 5th Corps of the Yugoslav People's Army. The Army of Republika Srpska was declared only on the 18th of June, 1992, so he had no authority over the JNA, their command and control, or that of the TO.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Stanisic states: "I'll call as many people as I can." Mr. Selak, do you know whether Stanisic had any authority or resources to address the situation in Western Slavonia? And please only answer to your own knowledge.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that Stanisic had any powers over the police and any of their organs in Western Slavonia. This sort of information did not reach military commands.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: So your testimony is that you don't know whether he did or not; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he did or not. I have no information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: The last question was about Mr. Stanisic's authority and resources. And now I'd like to know whether you know if Stanisic sent combatants to assist the JNA in the Western Slavonia operations.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were problems with Western Slavonia. Now, who took part there alongside the army, I can't tell you. There was chaos, people fled en masse to Banja Luka on tractors, whatever vehicles they could spare. They were in disarray. What the course of the operation in Western Slavonia was, I don't know, because I only provided logistics support to the JNA units. I was not aware of the way in which the civilian authority there was organised.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Further on, at the very end of this conversation between Karadzic and Stanisic, and I did not play the entire conversation for you so this quote is actually not part of what you heard. Mr. Stanisic said that he would: "Call my lads who are in contact with the TO Staff up there in Psunj [Realtime transcript read in error "Slunj"]." Psunj is near Pakrac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Were you aware that the Serbian DB members maintained contact with TO staff in Western Slavonia during the time that the 5th Corps was engaged in operations there?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that sort of information. The 5th Corps security organ did not inform me about me [as interpreted]. He was in communication with TO units and civilian security organs. I don't know anything about it, and I wouldn't want to go wrong. I would tell you on a personal note that they did, but that's just my personal view, and I have no information to back it with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Harbour, there seems to be some confusion about the place you referred to. It's now on the transcript as "Slunj." But it reads in the exhibit Psunj, P-s --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let's be -- yes, it may have been your pronunciation. But what we find in this transcript of the telephone conversation, right or wrong, that is also a matter which perhaps may need some verification, is that Mr. Stanisic would have said: "I called my lads who are in contact with the TO Staff up there on," it says "on," not "in," "Psunj," P-s-u-n-j, which as I do understand is a mountain in the south-west Slavonia region. Did you understand the question to refer to Psunj or to Slunj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My understanding was that it had to do with Psunj. I saw it in the transcript and that's how I understood it. Maybe I misheard it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of fact, in the transcript, on our transcript of today, it's Slunj, and your pronunciation might have caused a bit of a problem. But it's clear now that we're talking about Psunj and nothing else. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, yesterday, we reviewed some maps outlining your area of responsibility. And I just want to confirm with you that as commander of the 993rd Logistics Base, this area that we've been discussing in Pakrac and Psunj, in this area of Western Slavonia, was within your area of responsibility, was it not?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask Mr. Laugel to play another intercept for you. And this is P676 and records another conversation between Karadzic and Jovica Stanisic, and that's on the 20th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: For your information, it's the Prosecution's case that the person addressed as Joco in this intercept is Mr. Jovica Stanisic. Since it is difficult to follow who is speaking without the transcripts, would it be assist if we distributed the hard copies of the transcripts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that might assist. Of course all the parties in this courtroom can have it on their own screens. I mean, they can call for themselves P676 and have the transcript on the screen, so it would save some paper. But for those who have no direct access to e-court, there, it might assist.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I don't have a B/C/S transcript handy, so ... there's nothing to distribute to the witness, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And to the accused, apparently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll show it on the screen, although it will not help the witness very much if it is in English, unless the witness sufficiently understands the English language. Let me just ... And then you say you don't have a B/C/S transcript, which surprises me, because it is in e-court. So we can use it on the screen. So it is available. But it should be shown on the screen then, and then the ... The usher will assist.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Joco, hello" --

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Sorry, before we play it, I would just like to ask the interpreters pay particular attention to -- when interpreting the line that in the translation says the civilian, in parenthesis, as our language staff have had different views of how this is interpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you're asking our interpreters to verify the accuracy of a document which is in evidence, and there's an English version of that. So that is not usually done. But at least the Chamber is aware that there may be an issue there. If that needs verification it has to be sent to CLSS again to verify the accuracy of the translation in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I only know because we noticed this this morning, so just for the record today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That doesn't change the way in which it should be concluded. But we are now alerted to a possible issue about this part. And where exactly do we start? Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "R: Joco, hello. "J: Hello. "R: That's better. "J: How are you doctor? "R: Well, we're working. We're in a council meeting so I popped out to call you. "J: I'd like to ask you to tell you one thing which is that the situation around Okucani is critical tonight. "R: Critical is it? "J: Yes. "R: So they can take Okucani, or what? "J: Yes. "R: I have to call Slobo, right? "J: Well, I can do it. But I don't want to disturb him there right now. "R: Just feel free to call him. "J: What? "R: Feel free to call him. No, he has to know about this. He has to know about this. They mustn't be allowed to take hold of territory during a truce. Just call him up. "J: Good. Can't you do something for me here so that Krajina puts a bit of pressure there on? "R: No, no, can't be done because if -- "J: I mean to have the Banja Luka Corps. "R: No, if this Uzelac isn't there and Uzelac isn't there. "J: That's his deputy. "R: I beg your pardon. "J: He's got a deputy. "R: He can't do it without an order. I talked to him. He's a good man, but he can't do it without an order. "J: Well, let them fire a few rounds at night. Damn it. "R: He doesn't dare. "J: Huh? "R: He doesn't dare. I try to find him, but he won't dare to. "J: Come on, doctor, just a little. "R: I'll try but he won't dare to. Never mind, this should be reported to Slobo. Aco has finished that over there today. "J: Yes, yes, all right. "R: All right. Bye."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's note: It was too inaudible. We weren't able to hear what was said.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: In this intercept discussion, Karadzic and Stanisic both refer to someone named Slobo, and I would like to ask you if you know whether -- if you have any personal knowledge of whether Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Karadzic were in communication with Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I'm hearing this conversation, and I don't have any information about that. I have -- I had no information as to the sort of communication that they had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any dispute about the parties that the interlocutors, when talking about Slobo, would have referred to Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No. And there's no dispute that Stanisic was, on occasion, in touch with Milosevic either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from what seems to be almost obvious, I'm not saying that Slobo is -- in the conversations is usually, of course, always to be verified in the context, but is usually a reference to Mr. Milosevic, I would say. So, therefore, I think it would have been wiser to check with the Prosecution -- with the Defence whether there's any dispute about this reference here. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic asks at some point in this conversation: "Can't you do something here for me so that Krajina puts a bit of pressure there." And Mr. Karadzic responds that he will try. Mr. Selak, do you know, from your personal knowledge, if Mr. Stanisic had any ability to influence the combat instructions that were received by the 5th Corps?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, myself, had never heard that Stanisic had any sort of influence over the 5th Corps in Banja Luka. I suppose he did communicate with the corps command organs, but I don't have personal knowledge of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we don't have to -- what you suppose or not is -- it is about your personal knowledge. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: If we could now turn to Exhibit P1307, to page 5 in the English and page 6 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, this is a document that you looked at yesterday. And could I ask you to focus here on the experiences listed, once the document is displayed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Could we have page 5 in the English, please, and page 6 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Here, under experiences listed, the second item down states: "Some SDS leaders at all levels are seeking weapons from the JNA and the MNO of Serbia through various channels, in a fight for primacy ..." Serbia's Ministry of National Defence had its own access to weapons independent from the JNA; is that correct? And if you don't know, please just say so.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbian Ministry of Defence did not have weapons of its own. Weapons were stored in TO depots and JNA depots because there was, officially, the Yugoslav People's Army, and not the Army of the Republic of Serbia, at least officially. I don't know what the case was unofficially. Officially they were not supposed to have weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: But if they had access to weapons unofficially, they would have been able to supply weapons to groups without going through the JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Objection. It's an invitation to speculate. If -- if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's just ask the --

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I take your point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- witness whether he knows anything about -- but not knowing whether they had weapons at all, what -- if they would have had weapons how they would distribute them. That, of course, is, again, a matter at least -- what we would like to know is whether the witness could tell us anything about that in terms of facts rather than on -- in -- how that should have been. Yes? Do you know anything about distribution of weapons which may have come from the Ministry of National Defence of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: If we go down to the last line on this page in the English and onto the next page, which is page 7 in the B/C/S, this line reads: "In light of the fact that many people from the SDS are contacting the authorities and other structures in Serbia, it would be a good idea for the SSNO to point such occurrences out to the leadership in Serbia and to recommend to them to take more proactive steps to eliminate deviant behaviour in this region."

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: You've just heard an intercept of a conversation between Karadzic and Stanisic on the 4th of December, 1991, in which Stanisic agreed to supply men to assist in Western Slavonia? Would you consider that an instance of what is discussed in this document of a very prominent member of the SDS receiving assistance from an authority in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, objection. If the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Objection is sustained. Again, you're asking opinion from the witness. Is this a demonstration of that. Now we have this document. This document is -- clearly says something and we have another incident. Whether the one is an expression of the other, you can ask the witness whether he has any specific knowledge about that. But to say, Does this demonstrate what is seen there, asks for opinion and judgement, rather than facts. Please proceed. The Chamber will have to consider this question, perhaps, but it's not for the witness to -- unless the witness could tell us that his neighbour told him once that, in view of this document, someone else had expressed a certain -- that's facts. But you are just asking the witness to link two events. And that is judgement, opinion, assessment, rather than factual knowledge, unless the witness has any specific knowledge about the link between the document and the behaviour of Mr. Stanisic, as we have found it in the intercept. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, do you know of any instances that would exemplify what is being discussed here of the SDS contacting the authorities and other structures in Serbia? If you don't have any personal knowledge of these instances, please just let us know.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have this document. I have a whole batch of documents in my bag here. I have analysed it, but I have no direct knowledge about such communications, so I'm not really qualified to answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: In your Milosevic testimony, at transcript reference 22235 through -40, in reference to a document that is in evidence in this case as D271, you testified about convoys carrying materials, ammunitions, weapons and other items from Belgrade to Banja Luka after the JNA units in the area became VRS units. So after the 18th of May, 1992. And you testified that the vehicles from the 1st Krajina Corps that would be driven to Belgrade empty would then pick up toilet paper from a factory in Belgrade and then: "On the return journey that they should pick up material and equipment from the units of the Yugoslav People's Army on the territory of Yugoslavia, or, rather, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia." And then during your direct examination yesterday, two days ago, I believe, you testified that convoys of 30 to 35 trucks travelled from Banja Luka to Belgrade and back, carrying supplies from Belgrade on an almost daily basis. What was the time-period during which these convoys were making the trips to and from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, there's a dilemma here. When the toilet paper was mentioned, that factory was in Banja Luka, and they delivered goods to Serbia, so that was paper for Serbia. And from Serbia, the trucks constantly went in convoys not -- not convoys every day. Convoys went once or twice a month at the outside. Only individual trucks went daily. And they would bring weapons and ammunition, weapons not so often, ammunition and other equipment. And some of the weapons were transported even by air.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, you've already testified about that document and those -- and the route carrying the toilet paper and back in your Milosevic testimony. I'm interested in what time-frame you were referring to on your direct examination when you testified that 30 to 35 trucks travelled from Banja Luka to Belgrade and back, carrying supplies on almost a daily basis. What was the time-frame in which you were discussing?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the spring of 1992. In 1991, in December, convoys travelled other routes, such as via Tuzla as well. But speaking of Banja Luka, that corridor was very important. It was a life-line in the spring of 1992 when the Army of Republika Srpska was proclaimed, when the operations started, and the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina tried to cut off that route. Their Tuzla units were trying to cut off that route. And that's why we needed combat vehicles for escort of these convoys and aviation, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: In order to travel back and forth between Banja Luka and Belgrade, regardless of the route, these convoys containing ammunition and other weapons and other materials would have to cross the border between Serbia and Bosnia. And is it correct that the Serbian MUP had controls on the border?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, your answer was not audible. Could you repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The border crossing was at Brcko. It was called Srpska Raca. That was the border crossing between Serbia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's where the corridor went and the route convoys took. It was Srpska Raca. And it 1992, I travelled that route, and the police would check our documentation and there were even UN force there is; that is, a group of UN officers that also controlled the border at Srpska Raca. It was a bit illogical, incongruous. And I know from personal experience that there were abuses by the UN because when military transports travelled, they would move away from the border crossing, and the transports went through. What's interesting is the information, how the goods were camouflaged that went from Serbia to Bosnia and Herzegovina and vice versa. Custom seals were placed over the tarpaulin on trucks, and the goods declared would be one thing, and the actual shipment was fuel. So I -- I was there a couple of times, and I -- I was a witness of the transport of various goods.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: You've mentioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Harbour, you were talking about the trucks going empty to Belgrade, loading toilet paper there. I'm just trying to fully understand. And you refer to 22.235 to -240. What I read there is something different. Cellulose paper factory in Banja Luka by 1600 hours to load 100 tonnes of toilet paper. Vehicles spent the night over there. Next day at 6.30 the motor vehicles shall be collected at the work organisation, refueled, and shall set off for Belgrade at 700 hours and then to deliver that in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And the witness has also clarified that, I think. If my question was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you -- you -- well, you put it just the other way: Going empty to Belgrade and loading toilet paper. And I wondered what the basis for that question was, but apparently it was a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: It was a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Your Honours, my next question is the kind of question which you gave some guidance about yesterday. And I've carefully studied your guidance and I have endeavoured to craft the question accordingly. Once you've heard the question, I have prepared a brief submission regarding why I believe that the question should be asked the way that I've crafted it, and I leave it to Your Honours whether you'd like to hear my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Jordash will carefully listen as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, in your Milosevic testimony at transcript page 22257 which is e-court page 62 of Exhibit D699 in this case, Mr. Milosevic asked you if it was not the case that the VRS's approach to the conflict on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina was to "curb any possible incidents of conduct that could tarnish the dignity and reputation of that image." This is at -- Mr. Milosevic took these words from Exhibit D726 in this case. You responded at the same transcript page: "No, that was not the approach because 280.000 victims were not killed by individuals but by the army, paramilitary organisations, and volunteer units." Mr. Selak, based on your own personal knowledge and experience, do you have any information that would allow you to exclude that special units of the Serbian DB also contributed to these atrocities?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, from the end of the war, we, in the War Crimes Institute, have been studying documentation about the involvement of all the peoples, the Serbs, the Bosniaks, and all the others in the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. There were volunteers from all sides, and the personnel was provided in an organised way. We had documentation exactly how many people were involved. When I gave the number 280.000, we are still studying this number. It's probably lower, as we know now, but it is still 100- to 150.000. However, concerning the organisation of travels of -- of groups, and we have Kukanjac's orders about volunteer units, we know - we know for a fact - that groups from Serbia came in an organised manner. There is an order from the General Staff of the Yugoslavia army about units from the Uzice and Valjevo corps being involved in operations in Bosnia. When I reviewed the documentation that was ceased from the VRS here in the Tribunal, I found that document, among others, so these units from Serbia were involved in operations in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Doesn't answer your question, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: It doesn't exactly answer my question, Mr. Selak. I'm referring specifically to --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you kindly repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I will. Referring specifically to special units of the Serbian State Security Service in the Republic of Serbia, based on your personal knowledge, do you have information that would allow you to exclude that these units participated in the crimes that we've been discussing?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I did not have that information.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: And right now you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, that's -- that's a bit -- let me try to clarify the issue. In your testimony in the Milosevic case, you say, Those 280.000 were not killed by individuals, but they were killed by the army, by paramilitary organisations, and by volunteer units. Now, is there any fact known to you which would allow you to say that any of these units or entities you mentioned are not linked to the Serbian DB? Is there anything you'd say, Well, when I talk about the army, paramilitary organisations, and volunteer, I know for sure, because of this and this and this fact, that they were not in any way linked to the Serbian DB. Do you have any fact to your knowledge; or do you say, No, I do not have any facts which would allow me to say that they are not linked to the Serbian DB? Is the question clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question is clear to me, Your Honour. However, in this document, it says that the army distributed weapons to people. It doesn't say whether, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, or in Serbia, about 60.000 pieces of infantry weapons, and the document also says that the army agrees and approves of the formation of volunteer units that were not part of the Yugoslav People's Army, and it was those units that committed those crimes. And loads of them came from the Republic of Serbia. I know that for a fact. Unfortunately, it's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But again you say, I know that they came from the Republic of Serbia. Is there any fact known to you which would allow you to say, Well, they came from Serbia but they certainly were not linked in any way, they could not be linked to the DB; or do you say, No, I don't have such knowledge, which would then leave it open, whether or not they had been linked to the DB in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I repeat once again. The personnel that came from Serbia to Bosnia-Herzegovina, apart from military organisations, had to come with the knowledge of the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbia, because the MUP of Serbia always knew, had to know, who was leaving and who was crossing the border. And that's not military organisation. It was the civilian organisation. The Ministry of Interior, they monitor who is leaving and who is coming into the country. That's my argument. The army did not interfere with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You rightly say that's your argument. You are drawing inferences from what you know to be the system, without having any specific knowledge about links to the DB, but you say it hardly could be else, because they controlled the borders. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Harbour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Harbour. Then I suggest that we first take a break. After the break, how much time would the parties need? Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you allow me, ten to 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ten to 15 minutes. And, Mr. Jordash, could you give an estimate already.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: 20 minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 20 minutes. Then we'll take a break, and we resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Selak.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We did not have occasion to speak to each other and I will now move onto the topic I'm interested in. My learned friend asked you about volunteers and about whether you could rule out the possibility of volunteer units having been armed. Can we now call up P1312. You will tell me if you are familiar with the document; and, if you are not, whether you are familiar with some of the facts contained in that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 1, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: It is dated the 3rd of April, 1992. As it seems, it is the 1st Administration of the Federal Secretariat of National Defence that sent it to the General Staff of the armed forces of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Have you had a look of this page -- at this page?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Please focus on the preamble and item 1.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, are you familiar with the document?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have that document myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it true that the General Staff of the armed forces of the SFRY, in early April of 1992, issued an order to start forming staffs, detachments, and brigades of volunteer units as soon as may be, and that they be manned with the officer corps of the JNA, and that they be armed and equipped?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did this, in fact, come about?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Under the legislation in force at the time was it allowed for the JNA to recruit volunteers?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Volunteers were not part of the Yugoslav People's Army, but they were recruited in order to bring the manpower levels up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Harbour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac began with saying that this arose from questions about whether Mr. Selak could rule out the possibility of volunteer units being -- having been armed. In fact, we don't dispute that volunteer units were armed by the JNA. So this issue was actually not a part of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I may have misunderstood then. What was important, also, was the time-period when the arming effort took place in Bosnia. But I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, my learned friend from the Prosecution asked you if you could rule out the possibility that police units, too, were engaged in arming. And you answered that. I would like to have a quick look at 1D1995, which is related to the period that you spent on the field, 24th of April, 1992, and is related to your area of responsibility, i.e., Banja Luka. Can you tell me if you are familiar with the facts contained in the document? It is issued by the command of the 2nd Military District of the 24th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: It is sent to the Federal Secretariat of National Defence, its technical administration.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Of the Ministry of Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina: "We have received a request from the ministry, strictly confidential number 11, of the 23rd of April, 1992, for materiel and technical equipment to be used by the special purposes police detachment of the Banja Luka Security Services Centre." Next follows a list of equipment.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 88 items.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Precisely so, Mr. Selak.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: 88 items. Did you know that the MUP of Banja Luka, precisely for its own purposes, asked that it be furnished with weapons; also for the purposes of the special unit of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know if these -- this sort of equipment was delivered?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. The materiel and technical equipment requested here was delivered. I don't know if all. And I know that some of it came from the logistics base in Banja Luka, though I can't tell you specifically which items.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since the witness is familiar with the document and has confirmed his knowledge of these events, I would like to tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I have the document with me here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Isn't it true that you introduced it as an existing exhibit, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh. Let me see ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The previous one was an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The previous one, yes. This one then. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1995 will receive number D742, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, kindly tell us, if you remember, that there was the military post box 5042 in Banja Luka, or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do believe that there was such a military post box, but not in Banja Luka. I think it existed in Doboj. The Banja Luka Corps had a different post box. 5042, I think it was Doboj, but it's been a long time and it's difficult to remember these figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: It's all right, Mr. Selak. Do you know that in Doboj in this military post 5042 there existed a volunteer unit?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never in that area. I never visited the unit, so I can't confirm or deny it. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Selak. I have two or three quick questions for you. My learned friend showed you P626, which is an intercept that you looked at and commented upon yesterday. Can we have page 2? I'd like to check if we can clarify an entry. Mr. Selak, page 2 of the B/C/S. If you look at the third row from the bottom, Slobodan says: "It is of strategic importance for the future of RAM." Do you know what RAM is? What my question is for you is, what is the RAM?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a plan developed by the General Staff in Belgrade, which also included activities in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I don't know the details, but it was a well-known plan that had to do with combat and which outlined a political objective. I don't know the details, but the RAM plan was already around in 1992 or perhaps 1993, I'm not sure. I know of its existence, I didn't have it in my hands, but I discussed it with my colleagues at work. I don't know the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. During my colleague's cross-examination, I think that you said, at one point, that you fled Banja Luka for Germany but what the transcript does not reflect is the town or the country you travelled through to reach Germany.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Germany via Belgrade, rather, Srpska Raca and Belgrade, where I spent the night at hotel Moskva, and later on I joined my relatives. I spent 11 days in Belgrade and then I took the German plane, Lufthansa, to fly to Germany to join my son, and that was on the 1st of June, 1995. I spent some 13 or 14 days in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, did you know that a large number of Bosniak refugees were taken on into various refugee camps in Serbia, including Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were many refugees that found accommodation in Serbia but most of them were from East Bosnia because that was where there was the largest presence of paramilitaries who cleansed Eastern Bosnia or Bosniaks, and the Bosniaks fled, among other places, to Serbia. There was a camp in Zrenjanin, Belgrade, and Novi Sad, perhaps elsewhere as well. I know that people ran for their lives and fled to Serbia, among other places, though I say again most of them were from Eastern Bosnia which is close to the Serbian border.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Selak. My learned friend asked you, and you said that you supposed that the police forces were aware of volunteers joining JNA units. This is my question: At that time, in 1992, was it allowed for civilians to go to the theatres of war and join JNA units as volunteers? Was it possible under the law to stop a civilian who is unarmed from proceeding to join JNA units?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Yugoslav Presidency ordered that people be mobilised. But I have to give you the boarder information. The recruits who were serving their compulsory military service in the JNA, Bosniaks, Croats, Slovenians, left the ranks of the army. The army lacked personnel and volunteers were then admitted precisely because of the low strength of units, and it was expected that combat would follow. That was why the formation and arming of volunteer units was permitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: My last question, Mr. Selak: You said that, in Bosnia, some 68- or 69.000 pieces of weapons were distributed.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you consider that amount to be large; and was it sufficient for the arming of civilians; or was there need for additional arms?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I said yesterday that the amount was roughly 60.000, which would make up nearly four corps. This is something that we have recorded for. However, many convoys were stopped and weapons were seized, and none of it was recorded. And all of it was distributed to the Serbian people across Bosnia-Herzegovina, or perhaps I should say Republika Srpska because that was not the case of Sarajevo, Zenica, Tuzla, and so on. So all of it was distributed to the Serbian people, house to house, to volunteer units, to TO units, et cetera. People even dug up holes to hide weapons and, later on, these caches would be discovered, and this was forbidden.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Selak.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for allowing me to put additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Once the furniture is installed, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Just a few questions, if I can, Mr. Selak. I just want to pick up on the subject of the recorded conversations about events in 1991 in Western Slavonia and the impact on the Banja Luka region.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have on the screen, please, 65 ter 804. This is another intercept and this is a conversation between Karadzic and Uzelac. Not to be shown to the public, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And you'd like, when this comes on the screen, for you to read just the first three pages. I think the fourth page has the name of an operative on it, so if we can -- if we just stick with the first three pages. I want to try to, Mr. Selak, understand a little bit more about what was happening in 1991 in these areas. Please indicate when you want the next page.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And page 2 of the English, too, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have page 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, please. Thank you. And perhaps for the English, for Your Honours, if we could go to page 3 of the English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 4, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, at one point, Karadzic says - this is page 2 of the English and 2 of the B/C/S: "We have issued instructions to mobilisation everyone and to subordinate everyone to the command of the Yugoslav People's Army." And then a few lines down, Karadzic says: "It's important that some of those over 40, and others, remain, that some remain to protect the villages." This conversation took place in July of 1991. Do you know anything about the villages, which ones Karadzic may have had in mind, as in need of attention or defence?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the municipalities mentioned in this document and the majority population were Serbs. The operations were carried out in the area of Kupres which borders with the Republic of Croatia. There was combat going on there. Elements of my own unit were deployed to Kupres as logistics support. Men, up to 40, were supposed to respond to mobilisation call-ups and those over 40 were supposed to stay behind in their villages to protect them. Quite a lot of the population fled the area. There were people fleeing Banja Luka as well. We kept sending assistance to them. My commander, who was there himself, said that there were quite a few killings going on and that the police force was unable to deal with that on their own. It was the month of July of 1991 when we had conducted mobilisation. Many men in Banja Luka refused to respond to these call-ups, and we had to send military police patrols to go after them. There were quite a few such cases in Banja Luka, Your Honour, where Bosniaks and Croats refused to respond to call-ups and would then be searched and -- and there would be police sent after them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And why was a lot of the population fleeing the area; and why were people fleeing Banja Luka; and why were you sending assistance to them?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was fighting going on up there, as I said, in the direction of Croatia as well, and I had to provide support for these units in combat. And citizens were fleeing these areas where not only fighting that was lawful was going on, there was a lot of unlawful occurrences as well, causing citizens to flee. Unfortunately, later on, in 1992, there were quite a few people fleeing Banja Luka as well. But we are talking now about 1991 when there was fighting going on in Croatia, which became independent, but the army did not withdraw from all the garrisons. The Serbs formed their own authorities, and that was what caused the population to start fleeing, especially, as I say, the Croats and Bosniaks. I didn't bring along the census. I think I have it in my hotel room. I have the 1991 census that was carried out in Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. -- sorry to cut you, but there's just some further details I would like concerning what you've just said. You said: "The Serbs formed their own authorities, and that was what caused the population to start fleeing, especially, as I say, the Croats and Bosniaks." And when did that take place?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, there was fighting going in the month of July in Kupres and the border area with Croatia where units of the JNA and TO were engaged. This situation prevailed until the months of January or February 1992. I don't know when the fighting stopped. And then when Republika Srpska was set up, that was a different issue. So I don't know exactly when it all got resolved. I think it was the month of January or February.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Of which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So I do understand you correctly? You're saying it was January/February 1992 when the Serbs formed their own authorities, and that's what caused the population to start fleeing? It was in 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, on the 24th of October, 1991, the Assembly of the Serbian People proclaimed the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was when officially the process of legalisation began. It was not accepted that Bosnia-Herzegovina should secede from Yugoslavia. There was the wish to stay within Yugoslavia, and that was why, on 24th of October, 1991, the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was proclaimed. And I will never forget that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go to P673, please, the intercept we looked at before between Stanisic and Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Under seal, please. May I tender the last exhibit please Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] no objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Document 804 will receive number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Microphone, microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 804 will receive number D743, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D743 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Apparently we're in closed session, which I'm not sure -- no, we're not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This is an intercept you were shown before the break --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Harbour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Can I just verify that that's -- D743 has been admitted under seal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it has to be under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then it is -- the status is that it is a confidential exhibit under seal. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, you were the question about whether Stanisic seemed to be well informed about events in Western Slavonia, and you answered, Yes. And so I want to ask you about the -- those events and what made you conclude he was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, isn't it true that the question was whether, on the basis of this document, it seemed that, and then the witness said, Yes, and didn't I then say something about whether the witness had any personal knowledge or whether we --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And that's what I'm going to ask him about, whether he has got personal knowledge about some of the events discussed in -- in this intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understood that he had no personal knowledge. But if I'm wrong, then ...

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I believe he said he had no personal knowledge of Stanisic's knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That's right. And I want to ask him about the events in Western Slavonia that are referred to in this intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So apart from Mr. Stanisic's knowledge, whether the witness has knowledge about him, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let the questions be very clear on that because otherwise we get a long explanation on matters which may not reflect personal knowledge of the witness. So could you be very clear on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If you look at the first page there, Mr. Selak, and Karadzic notes, or -- sorry, yes. Karadzic notes the following: "From Banja Luka, 5.000 new people have arrived in Banja Luka. Ten thousand arrive tomorrow. I don't know why they are leaving, those -- those villages there." Are you able to cast any light on what Karadzic was talking about? Do you know anything about the arrival of 5.000 or 15.000 people in Banja Luka in December of 1991?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, people were fleeing Slavonia, Your Honours. Serbs were fleeing because of the fighting going on there. Croatia, at the time, was seeking independence, using also armed force to get it, and that's why people were fleeing Slavonia. At least part of the Serbian population were running for their lives, and they were in fear of the consequences of the fighting, and many of them came to Banja Luka. Your Honours, allow me to say one more thing. Even in 1995, everything was on wheels in Slavonia. Everybody was running to Serbia, but that was prevented. Peace was signed, and that didn't happen. But it was mayhem. People loaded all their belongings, all their furniture onto trucks, onto anything on wheels, trying to run to Serbia. But, eventually that didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's just move a bit further into the conversation between Karadzic and Stanisic. Page 2 of the English and 2 of the B/C/S. Karadzic notes there halfway down the English page -- no, further down the page towards the bottom: "They got as far as Pakrac. Up there are villages, man, they are villages there, from Podravska Slatina, from Bocina Gora. Everybody has out from Mount Bilogora, there's no one to protect them from that side, they were territorials there, there is no army there, that's the problem." Do you know what that is a reference to? Are you able to cast any light on that -- or those comments?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat: Civilians were fleeing because they did not feel safe staying on. They -- they were fleeing from the fighting in Sarajevo, in Banja Luka, and they were fleeing for their lives. Those were municipalities with a majority Serb population. They were afraid of the Croatian forces, and Vukovar later happened as well. There was mayhem. People were afraid of revenge, and I understand them completely. They had to run because the civilian authorities were not functioning. It was a combat area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But then let's go, finally, to page 5 of the English and 4 of the B/C/S. And Stanisic says, "they won't give up ...," this is halfway down the page in English: "They won't give up and there's no one there to protect them. They're scared stiff. Fucking hell. They are burning villages, killing, fucking hell, slitting throats. What?" And Karadzic says: "Yes." And then Stanisic, going over the page in the B/C/S, says: "We should have agreed to send all we could and raise -- raise of the volunteers possible there, raise them there." Do you know, Mr. Selak, whether, what is described there of villages burning and people having their throats slit, whether that has any basis, in fact, in December of 1991, and the need, as expressed by Stanisic, for some kind of defence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Harbour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Could I just ask that those be asked as two separate questions so it's clear to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the events described by Stanisic in terms of what was happening in some of the villages, burnings and slitting of throats, and so on?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the details. I know that was happening in the entire area but where exactly, when, I don't know. I did not have any detailed reports or information about actual events and who was responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: From your knowledge and experience of being on the ground during this period of time, did any of the Serb villages need protection from this kind of atrocity?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, that was the territory of Croatia, and the combat going on there was involving the JNA. It was responsible for these operations. If Croatia became independent, then the JNA should have pulled out and let the Croatian authorities to organise new government in those areas. However, the army did not withdraw. It got involved in two armed operations. Even volunteer units were formed. However, the Croatian forces were stronger, and then it all the resulted in a massacre, from which people were fleeing, as I described earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry. At what stages were the Croatia forces stronger; and at what stage did the massacre in relation to this commence?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to an order from General Adzic. In October 1991, General Adzic ordered me in Banja Luka to go tour Pakrac and Lipik together with Talic. And at that time, the rocket brigades from Banja Luka targeted Lipik and Pakrac with multiple rocket-launcher. There was not a single response from the Croatian side. However, that was in 1991. From then on, the Croatian forces advanced from Zagreb, Sisak, et cetera, to recover their territory from the JNA. We did not have details about these operations because it was the Banja Luka Corps that conducted them in addition to other units, and I don't know the details. But I know the outcome. Many people got killed because of what the JNA did. Because, in 1991, at a referendum in May, or maybe earlier, Croatia declared its independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, when did the Croatia forces advance from Zagreb? Are you able to put a month on that, please.
