utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you the exact months. They organised their own army in time. I don't know which unit was mobilised when, in what complement and what missions they had. I really don't know any of these things, because I didn't have access to that sort of information in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was it -- from what you have said, it was after October 1991. Was it within 1991?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, after October 1991. Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Within 1991?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It was after 1991 -- sorry. After October 1991. But was it still within 1991 when the Croatian forces advanced and the massacre occurred?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions. Thank you, Mr. Selak.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jordash. Any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since the Bench has no further questions either, Mr. Selak, this concludes your testimony in this Court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming the long way to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I'd like to wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, if this would be a suitable time to make the submissions you intended to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. The submission related to two expert reports, a MUP report and a military report. And the Prosecution has some very serious concerns about the format and the way that we must deal with these reports and wants to raise them. I'm going to ask Ms. Marcus to deal with the MUP report and then Mr. Weber to deal with the military report. I will ask Ms. Marcus to address you now on the MUP report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, thank you. With respect to the MUP report and for the information of the Chamber, the Prosecution has had to invest substantial time, I would say approximately two weeks thus far, just trying to determine what source material has been provided and what is still pending. When we request this material from the Defence we often receive only partial responses with comments upon the importance of our requests, thus, requiring repeated correspondence over one document or one footnote to try to convince the Defence to provide us with the sourced material. I find it surprising, to say the least, that the Defence should put forward a proposed expert report, fail to provide all the source material, and then oblige the Prosecution to convince them that the source material should be provided. Furthermore the latest response we received on the 10th of February from the Defence informs us that we will receive additional feedback from Mr. Milosevic early this week - that would have been this week - we're still waiting for that. Then we will need to sit down, compare the material and information provided by the Defence with the information provided by Mr. Milosevic, and again determine what materials are still missing. I will not take more time on this issue. We will be sending another communication to the Defence with a chart of the correspondence on each footnote and each source document. I don't see any other way to do that. I would just like to point out that this process is so time-consuming that we have not been able to get to analysing the report itself due to the substantial amount of missing material and challenges in receiving that material. One more point on the MUP report I'd like to raise, namely the inclusion in this report of portions which are irrelevant by -- according to the Defence and which will not be relied upon by them according to their own assertions. In an e-mail of the 10th of February the Simatovic Defence asserted: "In your letter you request documents only mentioned in the report for the sake of clarity of pleading and general context. We do believe that these documents are irrelevant for the case and will only burden the case file without any real necessity. We do even offer to omit sentences where these documents are mentioned." In the e-mail of the 18th of January, the Simatovic Defence had identified portions of the MUP report on which the Defence will not rely and other portions which are "of very limited relevance." Due to the time being invested in figuring out the missing information in relation to these reports, we submit that this time should not be spent on portions which the Simatovic Defence themselves will not rely on or which they already concede are irrelevant. The Prosecution submits that the Simatovic Defence should first be obliged to remove those portions of each report - well, my colleague will discuss the military report -- to remove those portions of the MUP report on which they do not intend to rely or which they have determined are not relevant. I now pass the floor to Mr. Weber for the military report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good morning. The Prosecution at this time provides a submission with respect to the proposed military expert report provided on 9 February 2012. The Prosecution refrains from using the author's name of this report due to a pending motion for protective measures filed on 30 December 2011. We do maintain our opposition to this individual being extended the requested protective measures. As part of this submission, the Prosecution does seek clarification from both Defence teams as to whether the military expert report is submitted as a joint report from both Defence teams. The Prosecution notes that section D1 of the introduction of the report which is 2D1066 states: "The report has been prepared only and solely for the needs of the Defence teams," plural, "in Court" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, can we just ask if it is a joint report, yes or no, then we get a yes or a no answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. The Prosecution would then like to place the following procedural history on the record at this time: On 1 April 2011, the Trial Chamber issued a Scheduling Order requiring the Defence to comply with disclosure obligations by 7 June 2011. In a motion filed on 6 June 2011, the Simatovic Defence requested an extension of time to disclose the reports of two expert witnesses. This included the military expert report. In paragraph 17 of the 6th June 2011 motion, the Simatovic Defence stated that it anticipated having the B/C/S version of its military expert report by 23 July 2011 with the English translation to be made available no later than 12 August 2011. On 16 November 2011, the Prosecution was sent a 732-page version of the report in B/C/S. The cover page of the report contained the date of November 2010. Based on this date, the Prosecution does not understand and still does not understand the reason the Defence waited to submit such a large report for translation when it appears that it was available to them - meaning both Defence teams - in November 2010. Or, for that matter, why the Defence teams did not disclose the report to the Prosecution as required on 7 June 2011. On 17 November 2011 the Simatovic Defence filed an update and stated the military expert report had been completed and submitted for translation on 4 August 2011. CLSS stated that the translation should be completed by the end of the year. The Prosecution notes the difference in the dates provided by the Defence on 6 June and 17 November and submits the likelihood of receiving an English translation of a 732-page report by 12 August was very low, especially if it was just submitted for translation on the 4th of August, 2011. On 9 February 2012, the Prosecution received notice of the expert report pursuant to Rule 94 bis and the availability of an English translation of the report. Upon initial review, it appears the current B/C/S version of the report is 768 pages. The corresponding English translation totals 1.105 pages. There appears to be a total of 3.178 different footnotes along with 130 appendices to the report. It does not appear that the Defence has disclosed the English or B/C/S version of the appendices. With respect to these appendices, the Prosecution would note that the references to them in the report appear to indicate these attachments include charts, figures, diagrams, and additional sections of the report that discuss matters such as "logistic support in the JNA, TO OS SAO Krajina, the establishment of the TO SAO K operation zones, Western Slavonia TO, and TO of local Serbs in Croatia" just to name some examples from parts 1 and 2 of the report. In paragraph 5 of the Prosecution's response dated 10 June 2011 to the Simatovic Defence request for an extension of time to file its expert report, the Prosecution submitted applicable law based upon the Rules of Procedure and Evidence and jurisprudence from the Gotovina Trial Chamber. This paragraph stated: "Rule 94 bis (A) requires a party to disclose the full statement and/or report of any expert witness within the time-limit prescribed by the Trial Chamber. The jurisprudence indicates that while this time-limit is not absolute, late disclosure of an expert report warrants the same considerations as the additional of documents to the Rule 65 ter exhibit list. The Chamber must therefore determine whether it would be in the interests of justice to consider a belatedly filed expert report by considering (A) whether the report is prima facie relevant and probative; (B) whether the party submitting the report is shown good cause for the belated submission; and (C), the extent to which the new filing would create an additional burden upon the opposing party. The Prosecution submits that this very standard should apply to the military expert report submitted by the Defence on 9 February 2012. The Prosecution submission would be there is a lack of good cause. This individual has been retained as an expert by the Defence teams since 2007 as reflected on the 8 May 2007 65 ter conference transcript, page 372. The reports appear to have been drafted by November 2010. The Prosecution submits that based upon these facts which have become known in terms of the timing of the report during the past few months, the Defence lacks good cause for the belated submission of the report. The Prosecution further submits that large portions of the report do not appear to be of central relevance or probative of issues in this case. As an example, the Prosecution would observe that part 2 of the report entitled "The SFRY OS VJ and the conflict in Croatia 1991 to 1995" contains discussions on the co-operation and co-ordination of tasks to the Main Staff of the VJ and the relationship between the Command Staff of the VJ and the SVK. There also appears to be a discussions of a variety of combat operations and units for which the relevance is unclear based upon the pre-trial brief of the Simatovic Defence. The Prosecution also note sat the time that there appears to be redundant material and analysis between the Defence report and the Theunens report. In particular, we would note at this time the decisions of the military laws and also the existence and use of temporary joint combat or ad hoc formations. The Prosecution would incorporate also the same concerns that have been articulated for the MUP report. With respect to the military expert report, going forward, in that there is likely to be correspondence or communications that could arise about whether or not large components of this report are of limited relevance or no relevance to this case. The submission of such a large expert report at the very end of the case creates and extraordinary burden on the opposing party under these circumstances. First, the Prosecution has great difficulty in navigating the report since the page numbers and the table of contents do not correspond to the page numbers of the English translation. In light of the fact of that this is a very voluminous report, this often causes great time in locating different sections of the report. Second, there are over 1600 different sources, many of which appear voluminous in and of themselves. These sources are referenced in over 3.000 footnotes. The Prosecution is still in the process of evaluating the amount of time necessary to process this report, but at this time, we can state that without the means of cross-referencing 65 ter, ERN, exhibit numbers, and just the descriptions of the documents, it will be very difficult to prepare such a large report in an efficient manner. The Prosecution also sees there are hundreds of footnotes without any 65 ter, ERN or exhibit number. Spot-checks have also revealed that we are not in possession of a significant amount of English translations for the underlying source documentation. It appears that the report may contain large volume of evidence that is not admitted and possibly not on the 65 ter lists of the parties. In light of the variety of units and operations discussed in the report and the documents the Prosecution may also possess, to contextualise these matters, the potential volume of material in this case, could greatly increase at a very late stage in the proceedings. The Prosecution is concerned over these circumstances. In light of the unclear relevance of some of the materials and lack of notice by the Defence, the Prosecution is generally unsure of how the Defence intends to rely on many of the materials or opinions referenced in the military report. Accordingly, the Prosecution respectfully requests at the very least the following from the Trial Chamber: First, a stay of the Prosecution's 30-day response deadline pursuant to Rule 94 bis until the Defence provides complete B/C/S and English versions of the entire report, including all appendices. Second, the Prosecution requests that the Chamber require the Defence to file a joint -- well, in this matter since it is not -- since the Stanisic has indicated that it is not a joint report, that the Simatovic Defence file a submission addressing the good cause for filing the report at such a belated stage and explain the relevance of the different sections of the report to their cases. It would be appreciated if in doing so the Simatovic Defence could directly reference where in their pre-trial brief they provided any notice to rely on such information contained in the report. If there is no clear relevance or no clear notice that have been provided, the Prosecution requests that either the Simatovic Defence withdraw those portions of the report or that the Trial Chamber strike those portions of the report based upon submissions by the parties. There are a number of other technical matters that are similar to what was raised with respect to the MUP report. In order have a clear record of many of these individual items, the Prosecution anticipates also sending a letter with respect to the military expert report, and we intend to copy the Chamber on this in order to keep the Chamber aware of the situation. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm not going to detain the Court with a response because obviously that concerns Simatovic. But I am responding to the suggestion that we, as Defence teams, should have disclosed the report to the Prosecution as required by 7th of June 2001 [sic]. I don't know of any Rule which requires the Stanisic Defence to disclose a report that it does not seek to rely upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's on the record. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me first give an assurances to the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber. At some point my learned friend Mr. Weber said that perhaps this was ill-intended on the part of the Defence. Wells let me reassure you that this there is no ill-intention on the part of the Defence. We are doing our best to provide adequate Defence for our client whilst co-operating with the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber. Mr. Weber said quite rightly that this expert report has been on our list since 2007. I wish to remind my colleagues from the Prosecution and Their Honours that the entire Defence team for Simatovic -- almost the -- in fact, the entire Defence team was -- had to change in 2009 due to a tragic circumstance. I do not want to be seen as if I were shifting this to anyone else, but we were doing our best to rise up to the challenge and grapple with the case. There did come about a misunderstanding because we thought that this joint expert report, who was on the list in 2007, we thought that this expert would end up on the Stanisic witness list. We don't want to say that it was the fault of the Defence for Stanisic. Rather, by the time we noticed that the expert witness was not on the list, we tried to get in touch with him, obtain his report, and file it. It is also true that my estimates with regard to the translation were wrong. We thought it would be much faster. We were waiting for the translation to be completed until several days ago, when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, let me just -- a lot of words. 23rd of July, you say, English translation, that's at least what Mr. Weber said, is to be expected on the 12th of August. How could you possibly have thought that 730 pages would be translated in two and a half weeks during the summer recess? I mean, we thought it would be much faster. Explain to me what experience you have which would allow you to expect reasonably a translation of 6 -- 730-page document within two and a half weeks. Could you please explain to me on what basis you could have thought that it would be any quicker than three, four, five months?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I simply have no explanation for that or justification. I gave that estimate lightly, obviously. I don't know what the resources or -- at the disposal of the the translation service are. We were -- we were given back some translations quite soon after we had requested them, and that led me to believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Translations of documents of what size? Three pages? Four pages? We're talking about 730 pages, Mr. Bakrac. So even to come up and say, Well, sometimes we receive translations rather quickly. Are you not taking it seriously when we put this question to you when you say, Well, we sometimes receive it very quickly. 730 pages, to give an expectation to receive in the middle of the summer recess, a translation within two and a half weeks, you should not have said that without having consulted with CLSS. And I take that if you would have consulted with them, that you would not have had any reasonable expectations to have received it within two and a half weeks in the middle of the summer. Please proceed, and try to focus on the core. I consider the bad intents to be rather in the margin than in the core. The primary concern of the Prosecution is how can we possibly deal with this material at this stage, and isn't the Simatovic Defence to be blamed for this situation to arise. That's the issue. Could you please focus on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that my colleague, Mr. Petrovic, was in communication with Ms. Marcus, and in their exchange, he suggested a meeting. Perhaps the most expedient solution would be, if you agree, that we meet next week with our colleagues from the Prosecution and try and resolve the matter in practical terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When did Mr. Petrovic suggest a meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in a letter, dated the 10th of February --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's three years too late, approximately, isn't it? When the expert was tasked in 2007 or 2006 or 2007, then to say, Well, let's resolve the matters. The problem is huge. And to say, We'll meet and then the matter will be resolved is of a similar kind as to say on the 23rd of July that there will be an English translation by the 12th of August. I admire your optimism. Please proceed. And by the way, what was the answer by Ms. Marcus or ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that -- that offer was with respect to the MUP report. It was in an e-mail communication regarding some details of footnotes in respect of the MUP report. I would just add that this problem that we have with the military report certainly cannot be resolved in a meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems that it's unlikely. Has any suggestion been made to resolve the matter in a meeting, as far as the military report is concerned? Did you ever offer that, Mr. -- or did Mr. Petrovic offer that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Several days ago, we sent the translation of the expert report to the Prosecution, and we are still reviewing the footnotes and annexes to see what is missing. I will deal with this as soon as possible and get in touch with the Prosecution to see which are the portions that we can delete, in order to make this large expert report acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, could you tell us. Mr. Weber told us that you indicated to the Prosecution that you would not rely on portions of the police report, the MUP report. Could you tell us approximately how many of these 180 pages you would not rely on? No, I'm not asking for -- but would it be one-third, or half, or 20 per cent or -- approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am in a position now where I may say something that would be imprecise. Can I have some time, please, to review that and get back to you with an accurate figure of what it is that we can set aside as the portion that we will not be relying on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you indicated that to the Prosecution, isn't it? So you must have an idea about it. That's at least what Ms. Marcus told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. That concerns the police report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm asking about the police report, because I referred to 180 pages, which is the police report, Mr. Bakrac. So what did you have on your mind when you communicated to Ms. Marcus that you might not rely on certain portions of the police report? I take it that you had identified them, at least to some extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, they are portions related to the situation in Kosovo in 1989, Presidency decisions, that's to say SFRY Presidency decisions, to deploy the JNA to Kosovo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you have identified them. Could you tell me approximately what portion of the report that presents? Again, is this 20 per cent; is this 50 per cent; is it 40 per cent; is it 80 per cent? Approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I assume -- again, I don't want to go wrong. Let's say approximately 30 per cent of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the same for the military report.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that there is background noise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you will allow me, the military report, if I may address you on that on Monday and give you an estimate because -- so to give you an estimate of what is the portion that we believe is not relevant for the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So apparently there is a portion which is not relevance for the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we received the military report as a whole. There are elements in it related to the historical chronology of the JNA. And for the sake of expeditiousness and to allow adequate preparation to the Prosecution, we can check this with the expert. We are going to be editing his report so I suppose we have your understanding for the fact that we will have to consult with him to see and establish what are the portions that we can leave out. We will be focussing on those elements that are not strictly necessary for our case, and we will do so in consultation with the expert, and we would kindly ask you to give us a time-limit within which we would go through the exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, what is relevant for the case is for counsel to decide. What portions not to rely on, relevant or not, is for counsel to decide. Now it sounds very pleasant to say "for the sake of the expeditiousness and to allow adequate preparation to the Prosecution," if you would have consulted and have made up your mind once you received the military report, which was in July, you would saved this Tribunal a huge amount of -- and money and time by selecting the relevant portions you wish to rely on before you sent it to CLSS for translation. So, on the basis of what you've told me now, it is a total misapprehension to think that sending everything for translation would either speed up or would accommodate the Prosecution. I'm inclined to believe that the contrary is true; that it delayed, considerably, the availability of an English version of the report. Now, the Chamber has earlier expressed that it would be necessary that you consult -- that you seriously consider to reduce the size of the report. From what I see now, that no serious effort has been made in that respect because the numbers here are still the same as they were half a year ago. Of course the Chamber could give no guidance because it had no access to the content of the report, apart from that it's not for the Chamber to decide what you consider to be relevant for the case. Finally, of course, we'll decide whether evidence is relevant or not, but we are usually rather generous, expecting that the parties will seriously take efforts not to flood the Chamber with irrelevant material. The Chamber is not inclined very much to be the master of the case presentation. To the contrary, it's in the hands of the parties, and the Chamber expects the parties to responsibly perform their task. Now, there is some background noise. I was -- I don't know where it comes from. I'm not aware of doing anything wrong, but there seems to be a ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, again, it seems that I am to blame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, I would approach it in a different way, Mr. Bakrac. I would say at least this problem is resolved. That's the positive approach. Mr. Bakrac, do you know what you're risking at this moment? You're risking that the Chamber will not admit, for procedural reasons, the evidence you want to present. And looking at this history of this problem where the expert was tasked in either 2006 or 2007, where you have, from what I understand from your submissions at this moment, that you have not seriously followed the guidance of the Chamber. That is, see how we can reduce it, take care that everything is transparent. You're taking high risks because there are limits to what a Chamber can do, and you know what the case law is. And, of course, I first will have to consider with my colleagues what the consequences are, but it should have been clear to you already for well over a half a year that you should do something, which apparently you haven't done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Judges will have to consider the situation. Meanwhile, even if one meeting might not resolve the problem, certainly not in respect of the military report where there seems -- the problems seem to be even greater than with the MUP report, that it might be good to see to what extent a meeting can contribute to a solution such as identify where there is an overlap with the Theunens reports and no great dispute about the content - I do not know. I have not seen the report. I have not read it, I should say - and to see whether we can get the problem back to such dimensions that there is a reasonable chance that the matter will be resolved, because the dimensions of the problem at this moment seem to be such that unless something drastically is done that it might be extremely difficult to come to an acceptable solution. Mr. Weber, let me first -- Mr. Bakrac, not just a meeting on the MUP report but on the military report as well. Tea or coffee, I leave that to you. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to the military report, the scope of the problem is such that we aren't even in a position to really dive in depth in terms of how to analyse this or even organise it because we're completely lacking means of cross-referencing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, if Mr. Bakrac, after having gone through the -- the table of content of the report would come to you and would say, Would it assist you in any way if I would drop this chapter, that chapter, that chapter, that chapter? How could we continue to work on chapter A and would it be agreeable to you that we start with chapter 7 A and then deal with chapter 3, and could we make an offer within the next week explaining to you where the overlap with the Theunens report is, why not?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that. With respect to that possibility, the Prosecution would like to reiterate that it considers that as inappropriate for us to decide or participate in deciding what the Defence considers that they need to rely upon in the submission of its own case. And, as the Chamber stated, this is incumbent upon the Defence to decide to do that. In my original submission, I also stated that it is unclear to us, based on the notice that we received from the Defence, what many of these portions may or may not be relevant to. So it would be the Prosecution's position that it is the Defence's decision alone to decide what they intend to rely upon and they are the ones best positioned to do that. The Prosecution does not seek to engage in a negotiation with them over what may or may not be relevant to the case. I believe that would be unproductive and also time-consuming with such a voluminous report. Not to say that we wouldn't be willing to meet with them to discuss many of the technical matters, table of contents, see how we can better organise going through the report, we would be willing to do that, and that could alleviate some ability for the parties to -- with whatever is decided to then be submitted be able to more efficiently process the report on that level. The Prosecution would just note we've been discussing the possibility of deadlines. We would request that firm deadlines be set upon the Defence to make decisions with respect to both the MUP report and the military report, as to what portions are going to be relied upon. The Prosecution also would, with respect to the military report, again reiterate that we have requested two specific forms of relief, and, one, that being a stay of the Prosecution's 30-day response deadline and also whether or not the Defence can file a submission based on what the relevance is. So we would again request that the Chamber consider that as part of its deliberations. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What I heard over the last two and a half minutes, Mr. Weber, is to say, Whatever the Chamber suggests would not be appropriate, we couldn't do that, we couldn't negotiate that. I try tried to give you some guidance on what such a meeting could mean. What you say, Of course, we could meet but only on technicalities, apparently not accepting the guidance and the suggestion of the Chamber. Because what I suggested is that a meeting, not primarily focussing on only on the technicalities, might assist in down sizing the problem in such a way that perhaps in the near future that we could better tackle the problem. Of course, you couldn't impose on the Defence what they should rely on yes or no. But, of course, you can say, If you do not rely on that part of the report then we would have a lesser problem. Of course, that -- relevance and relying on certain portions which something you could not possibly discuss between the parties seems far too strong statement to me. And what you then did is insist on getting a decision on what you wanted. Of course, finally the Chamber will decide on any motion, but the Chamber would appreciate if would you also first try to explore a bit more in detail the possibilities that may lead to a solution. At the same time, Mr. Bakrac, I think that the message I conveyed to the Simatovic Defence has been strong enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. And if I may be allowed to add, I did have the intention of the Defence sitting down and seeing what it is, at this stage of trial, that we can leave out of the report and then perhaps see what it is that the Prosecution find controversial and complete the exercise as soon as possible. That was my suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think I earlier expressed that the path to the place where we don't want to be is paved with good intentions. I have heard a lot of good intentions in the context of the matter that we're discussing at the moment, and I'm afraid that we are at a point that good intentions are not sufficient anymore and that decisions will have to be taken and it comes down to, now, decisive steps to be taken. Anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We will sit and meet with the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, my suggestion to you would be to very well consider your position at this moment. Not to meet within a half an hour from now, but, first, make up your own mind, then met with the Defence [sic], and the Chamber expects a very brief report ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As always, the Chamber offers its good services as well. The Chamber's team will go through all the submissions which were made in relation to these reports over the last long period of time and may offer its assistance in resolving matters, and that is done by Chamber's staff, independently, and not on specific instructions from the Chamber. Don't be afraid that the Chamber is intervening or interfering with matters which are primarily in the hands of the parties. At the same time, the Chamber cannot go on just to look and listen. And of course, finally, the Chamber will decide the matter, if need be. But if we could -- the Chamber is always anxious to achieve that both parties will be able to present their cases in the best possible way but within the limits of what is procedurally acceptable. So if Chamber's staff would offer any assistance, it may be by identifying what issues have been put on the record, whatever, not in any way to attempt or even try to attempt to control what parties should present. But since it is finally a decision of the Chamber whether or not evidence can be admitted, yes or no, and in view of the -- what I just expressed as the -- what is important for the Chamber, that is, that within procedural limits, parties are able to optimally present their cases, it is in this context that you should understand any communication with Chamber's staff. We are running out of the tape, I take it. If there is any other urgent matter to be raised at this moment. If not, then we adjourn, but not -- no. I'll communicate this matter in an informal communication with the parties. And we will adjourn until Tuesday, the -- no. Yes, 21st -- 21st of February, quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon, in this same courtroom, II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
